title: Italian politics of the 1970s-80s and a childhood of frugality
summary: He compares Italy's terrorism-era politics with today's anxiety, recalls limited TV, saving electricity, and no phone or hot water until age seven.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Every once in a while in this country we read about Italian politics. And you know they have their share of issues and scandals and so forth. As that is your native country I wonder how our politics compare to what you grew up with?

Well the scandals were always there. And I think that in the 70s and the early 80s the situation was even much worse because we shouldn’t forget that we had the problem of internal terrorism in Italy. So we had organized crime that was killing judges almost every week you know. One of our prime ministers, Aldo Moro, was killed by the extreme left movement. So we had terrible things happening way worse than today. But again, for some reason, you know I was little so I don’t remember much, but my parents, when I talk to them they say that there was a joy of living. You know? Even though they would blow up every now and then a train station, blow up a square in Milan, you know and people getting killed like that. But no one felt oppressed by this kind of anxiety that we are feeling today. Even though those times now, watching now, they seem to be worse and more dangerous than now. So again, what is that? You know I think you have a point, it’s just the fact that all day long people are watching TV and being bombarded. Because back then a TV would be — that’s another issue — we would turn on the TV only in the evening, having dinner, watching the news. And maybe in the early morning before going to school they had a little show of cartoons that we would watch as kids. And then in the afternoon we would come back from school and we were allowed maybe one hour to watch TV in the afternoon. Otherwise we would turn it off. And we would turn it off even because there was an awareness about the consumption of electricity you know. I remember my grandmother, I used to have one of those cute electric trains, you know, that my father bought for us. And once I took it to my grandmother and so I plugged it in, I put it together and I started playing. And then after about a half hour my © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

grandmother said, “Now we stop because the electricity is expensive.” And that was perfectly normal. We accepted that. Now if you tell a kid, you know, now you stop doing the videogame because the electricity is expensive, they are looking like you’re crazy. They’re going to call the number, 9-1-1, say my father is going crazy.
I know the power went out in our house the other night and it was like what do we do? It was like a crisis.

Yes, but think, we are talking about not that long ago you know, the early 80s, I was 6, 7, 8 years old. And this was our life. Everything, nothing would go to waste. Nothing would go to waste. And I’ll tell you one more thing. And I’m not afraid of sharing some very personal matters. In the first apartment that I remember living with my parents, that is where I was born, we didn’t have a telephone. We got our first landline phone I think when I was 7 years old. And also until the age of 7 we didn’t have warm water. We only had cold water. So in the summer it wasn’t a big deal but in winter we would wash our faces with cold water in the morning and we would take a bath. My mother would put some big pots of water to boil you know, and then mix it with the cold water in the bathtub. And I did that until 7 and I don’t remember, I don’t remember no one of us ever complained about that.

Yeah. And we were always clean. Always clean. Always clean clothes. I can’t even tell you how things are changed, and in spite now we have a much more comfortable life but why is that that we feel so much nostalgic about those years? What is that?
